newsitem.title: USA: Whitewater prosecutor Starr to join university.
newsitem.headline: Whitewater prosecutor Starr to join university.

text.p: Whitewater prosecutor Kenneth Starr will become dean of a California university law school in August and apparently plans to step down from leading the probe, the university said Monday.

"It's going to be a gradual transition process. On or about Aug. 1, he will be assuming the full-time duties of dean," said Jeff Bliss, a spokesman for Pepperdine University in Malibu, California. Bliss said he understood Starr, 50, planned to step down as Whitewater independent prosecutor, a position he has held since August 1994.

The announcement came at a crucial time in the investigation of Whitewater, a complex probe that grew out of a failed real estate venture in Arkansas in which President Clinton and his wife were passive investors.

According to news reports, Starr's staff has been working on a memo outlining the pros and cons of bringing criminal charges against government officials, including Clinton, first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton and White House aides.

Monday's announcement led to speculation that Starr had decided not to seek indictments against Clinton or his wife, who have denied any wrongdoing. But Starr cautioned reporters not to read too much into the announcement.

"My decision has been guided entirely by a sense of what is a wonderful and right opportunity for me and my family. But in the meantime, I'm off to Little Rock this evening, and it's full steam ahead," Starr told ABC-TV as he left Washington Monday. Starr said much could happen between now and August.
The White House officially declined to comment on the development, but privately one Clinton aide said: "There are a lot of smiles around the White House."
Clinton's allies have accused Starr, who has doggedly pursued the Whitewater investigation, of having a Republican bias. The investigation has cast a shadow over the presidency of Democrat Clinton.
Some of Starr's critics said Monday they thought he might be stepping down because he has failed to find any firm evidence against the Clintons.

"I think the investigation is petering out," said David Williams, the attorney for Patsy Thomasson, a White House aide and longtime friend of the Clintons. Thomasson came under Starr's scrutiny as part of his probe into the suicide of deputy White House counsel Vincent Foster and the "Travelgate" firings at the White House travel office.
Williams said Starr's team has become more quiet in recent months. "Last summer they were hot and heavy but we haven't heard a peep from them since August last year."
In addition to becoming dean of the law school, Starr, a former U.S. solicitor general, will also head Pepperdine University's new School of Public Policy as its founding dean, the university said.

"Kenneth Starr brings a breadth of experience and knowledge that is virtually unmatched: he has been a judge, a prosecutor, an attorney involved in private practice and he has taught at our law school," Pepperdine President David Davenport said in a statement.

Starr won a victory in May last year when a jury in Little Rock, Arkansas, found businessman James McDougal and his ex-wife Susan -- partners of the Clintons in the Whitewater real estate development -- guilty of fraud charges.
Arkansas Gov. Jim Guy Tucker, who was not involved in the Whitewater land deal, was also found guilty of two charges.
But Starr suffered a setback last August when two bankers who were political allies of Clinton were acquitted by an Arkansas jury of fraud and conspiracy charges.
In 1983, Starr, then 37, became the youngest judge ever appointed to the federal appeals court in Washington. He left the court in 1989 to become solicitor general.
A native of Vernon, Texas, Starr left Washington at the close of the Bush administration, later joining the Washington office of the Chicago-based law firm, Kirkland & Ellis.
Starr replaced Whitewater independent counsel Robert Fiske in August 1994. He has also served as an adjunct professor at New York University's School of Law for the past five years.
